title: EVALUATING ARCHITECTURAL LEGIBILITY: Way-Finding in the Built Environment
research_question: To evaluate the legibility of university buildings, specifically assessing the nature and pervasiveness of way-finding problems, the relationship between way-finding behavior and familiarity, and the influence of visual/spatial features (especially plan configuration) on way-finding behavior.

participants.description: University of Michigan undergraduates, about equally divided among men and women. Approximately 25% first-year, 60% second-year, remainder in final two years. Minimum 6 weeks to 2 months on campus.
participants.recruitment: Enrolled in Psychology Department classes, fulfilling a course requirement for participation in an experimental study.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Ten university buildings on the Central Campus of the University of Michigan, varying in function (classroom/office/laboratory, administrative), height (3-4 stories, 8-11 stories), age (early 1900s to early 1970s), size (under 200 feet to over 500 feet), and floor plan configuration (I, L, T, V shapes, hollow squares). All had predominantly 'double-loaded' corridors.

Set of 30 highly simplified and abstracted two-dimensional diagrams of plan configurations. 20 diagrams were simplifications of actual University of Michigan buildings (including the 10 study settings), and 10 were additional variations constructed by manipulating corridor segments, symmetry, and corner intersections.

measures.instrument: Ratings by independent group of 20 raters on a 4-point scale (implied by mean range in Table 1, 'Complex' vs 'Simple' diagrams).
Ratings by independent group of 20 raters on a 4-point scale (implied by mean range in Table 1).
Ratings by independent group of 20 raters on a 4-point scale (implied by mean range in Table 1, 'Difficult' vs 'Easy' diagrams).
Ratings by independent group of 20 raters on a 4-point scale (implied by mean range in Table 1).
Ratings by independent group of 20 raters on a 4-point scale (implied by mean range in Table 1, 'Difficult' vs 'Easy' diagrams).
Question 1: 'How often have you had occasion to use - to be inside - this building?' (4-point scale: never, once or a few times, fairly often, regularly)
Question 2: 'How long has it been since the last time you were inside of this building?' (4-point scale: a year or more, a month or more, a week or more, a week or less)
Question 3: 'Roughly what percentage of the total building would you say you've been in?' (4-point scale: 25% or less, 25% to half, half to 75%, all or almost all)

Question 4: 'Have you ever had trouble finding your way or gotten 'lost' inside of this building? How often has this happened?' (4-point scale: just about every time, fairly often, just occasionally, practically never)
Question 5: 'What was the 'most lost' you've ever become in this building?' (4-point scale: totally lost, just momentarily disoriented)

measures.construct: Perceived Ability to Direct a Stranger
measures.instrument: Question 6: 'Do you think you'd be able to direct a stranger to many places (e.g. classrooms, stairways, exits) inside this building? How many places?' (4-point scale: practically nowhere, most anyplace)
Question 7: 'How confident would you be of the directions you'd give to such a stranger?' (4-point scale: not at all confident, quite sure)

measures.construct: Perceived Ease of Figuring Out Building
measures.instrument: Question 8: 'All things considered, do you find this building a relatively easy or a relatively difficult place to 'figure out' and in which to find your way?' (4-point scale: difficult, easy)

measures.construct: Perceived Ease of Drawing Building Layout
measures.instrument: Question 9: 'Do you think you could draw a quick diagram of this building's 'layout' showing the outline of the building and the arrangement of the corridors inside...? Would doing such a diagram of this building be difficult or easy?' (4-point scale: difficult, easy)
Question 10: 'How confident would you be of the building sketch you'd have drawn?' (4-point scale: not confident, quite sure)

findings.antecedent: Plan configuration judged as 'high simplicity' (based on abstract diagrams)
findings.consequent: Reported way-finding scores (mean frequency of disorientation)
findings.mechanism: Simpler plan configurations are easier to form a mental image of, facilitating way-finding.

findings.antecedent: Plan configuration judged as 'high describability' (based on abstract diagrams)
findings.consequent: Reported way-finding scores (mean frequency of disorientation)
findings.mechanism: Easier to describe plan configurations may indicate better mental representation, aiding way-finding.

findings.antecedent: Plan configuration judged as 'high plan legibility' (based on abstract diagrams)
findings.consequent: Reported way-finding scores (mean frequency of disorientation)
findings.mechanism: Higher perceived legibility of the plan directly relates to better way-finding performance.

findings.antecedent: Plan configuration judged as 'high preference' (based on abstract diagrams)
findings.consequent: Reported way-finding scores (mean frequency of disorientation)

findings.antecedent: Plan configuration judged as 'high memorability' (based on abstract diagrams)
findings.consequent: Reported way-finding scores (mean frequency of disorientation)

findings.antecedent: Judged simplicity of plan configuration diagrams
findings.consequent: Reported frequency of disorientation across 10 buildings
findings.mechanism: Simpler plans are easier to mentally represent, reducing disorientation.
findings.quote: A strong and significant relationship was found between judged simplicity of plan configuration diagrams and reported frequency of disorientation across the 10 buildings (r = .75, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Judged simplicity of plan configuration diagrams
findings.consequent: Variance in reported frequency of disorientation data
findings.mechanism: Simplicity of plan configuration is a strong predictor of way-finding behavior.
findings.quote: simplicity judgments, provided by a group of independent raters, were able to account for 56% of the variance in reported frequency of disorientation data.

findings.antecedent: Participants' own familiarity with study settings (specifically recency of usage)
findings.mechanism: Familiarity contributes to way-finding ability, but less so than environmental features.
findings.quote: participants' own familiarity with the study settings (specifically recency of usage) was able to account for but 9% of the variance in these way-finding scores.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with buildings (frequency, recency, extent of usage)
findings.mechanism: Familiarity alone does not simply explain disorientation across different settings.
findings.quote: Correlational analyses, based upon the 10 sample settings as cases, yielded no significant relationships.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with buildings (frequency, recency, extent of usage)
findings.mechanism: In some settings, familiarity mitigates way-finding problems; in others, it may increase opportunity to get lost.
findings.quote: While these yielded significant relationships for 5 of the 10 buildings, in only three cases was familiarity able to account for more than 10% of the variance in way-finding behavior; in no case was familiarity able to account for more than 25% of the variance.

findings.consequent: Way-finding problems (reported getting lost often or almost always)
findings.mechanism: A substantial minority of users experience way-finding difficulties.
findings.quote: Averaging across all 10 buildings, 9.1% of respondents at least minimally familiar with these settings report becoming lost often or almost always

findings.consequent: Way-finding problems (reported being quite or totally lost at least once)
findings.mechanism: A substantial minority of users experience way-finding difficulties.
findings.quote: 14.1% have been, on at least one occasion, quite or totally lost

findings.consequent: Way-finding problems (reported frequent and severe disorientation)
findings.mechanism: A substantial minority of users experience way-finding difficulties.
findings.quote: frequent and severe disorientation are reported by 8% of respondents.

mechanisms: Way-finding is a complex cognitive task that relies on storing information about specific locations and their spatial relationships in one's head. Visual/spatial variables like plan configuration impact the ease of forming these mental images.
Good form characteristics (symmetry, regularity, continuity) of a building's plan configuration facilitate the creation of a clear mental image, which in turn aids way-finding.
implementation_implications: Simple paper-and-pencil tests of plan configuration diagrams can be valuable for both postoccupancy evaluation and 'preconstruction simulation' to assess potential way-finding issues.
Designers should consider the simplicity and legibility of floor plan configurations to improve way-finding behavior in buildings.

tables.description: Results of Paired t Tests for Environmental Variables, showing mean scores for low and high groupings of plan configuration characteristics (Preference, Simplicity, Describability, Memorability, Plan Legibility) and their corresponding t-values and p-values.

limitations: Way-finding behavior assessment is based on self-report data, which may not fully correlate with objective measures of way-finding performance.
The study did not explore other behavioral consequences of illegible settings beyond way-finding.

paper_metadata.title: Evaluating Architectural Legibility
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: One potentially significant yet little investigated criterion for postoccupancy evaluation is the "legibility" of a setting—the degree to which a building facilitates the ability of users to find their way within it. The present study evaluated the legibility of a sample of ten university buildings. Self-report data indicated way-finding to be a problem for a substantial minority. The impact upon way-finding of several theoretically derived visual/spatial variables was also assessed. Two aspects of the floor plan configurations of these settings, as judged from highly significant relationships to frequency of disorientation. One of these variables, judged simplicity of floor plan configuration, was able to account for 56% of the variance in these data. One other potentially important variable, respondents' own familiarity with these buildings, was able to account for but 9% of the variance in frequency of disorientation data.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The legibility of an environment (e.g., clarity of structure, distinctiveness of parts) influences an individual's ability to navigate and form mental maps, thereby affecting way-finding performance.

mechanism_chain.description: Simpler or more legible architectural plan configurations reduce cognitive load and facilitate the formation of accurate mental maps, leading to improved spatial decision-making and reduced disorientation during way-finding.
